newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican peasants continue corn protest blockades.
newsitem.headline: Mexican peasants continue corn protest blockades.

text.p: Mexican peasants continued to man road blocks in the impoverished southern state of Chiapas Tuesday, protesting corn prices which they say are not high enough to feed their families.

Corn farmers from the regions of Villacorzo, Villa Flores, Angel Albino Corzo and La Concordia went into a 10th day of protest over floor prices set by the state government, a source from the National Farming Council (CNA) said.
The region is just south of the state capital Tuxtla Gutierrez and is a prime livestock and coffee growing area as well as having substantial corn production.
But the government is adamant that the state-fixed corn floor price, the limit low offered to growers, will remain at 1,270 pesos per tonne for the time being.

"The price will remain the same," Saul de la Torre, the state delegate for the federal staples agency, known in Spanish as Conasupo, told TV network Televisa. De la Torre claimed their were no funds available to offer more money.
Mexico sets state floor prices for corn and the government promises to buy up all the grain produced at that price from those growers who are unable to strike sales in the private sector.
The blockades are stiring tension in Chiapas, with cattlemen, dairymen and truckers all demanding the government break them by force because of the losses they are incurring.
Dairymen poured 55,000 litres of milk down the drains Monday in a symbolic counterprotest because they were unable to transport the milk to market, media reported.
Mexico City daily La Jornada said corn growers from five other towns, namely Laja Tendida, Flores Magon, Carranza, Sitala, Amatenango de Valle, also started road blockades on Monday.
Government tactics for the moment, media reported, were to continue negotiations with the protesters to try and solve the differences without the use of force.
But given the stance that no additional funds are available to pay higher prices, if a compromise is not reached soon "actions will be taken within the limits of the law," La Jornada reported.
